newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government seeks to reverse poll slide.
newsitem.headline: Australian government seeks to reverse poll slide.

text.p: Australia's government, hammered in the polls by corruption scandals and a land rights row, will turn to its grassroots to rebuild support midway through its first term, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Tuesday.

A newspaper poll showed the conservative Liberal-National coalition's lead over the Labor opposition had dropped to five percent -- less than half the 12-point advantage it enjoyed just a few months ago.

Fischer said the coalition, which ended 13 years of Labor rule with a landslide 1996 election win, had turned the economy around but had been dragged down by public anger over abuse of parliamentary benefits and the Wik land rights row between Aborigines and farmers.
The government had underestimated the impact of the two issues and would use parliament's winter recess to rebuild its support, Fischer told reporters.

The government was hit earlier this year over allegations of abuse of allowances against independent senator Mal Colston -- whose vote was crucial to government legislation passing the hostile upper house, the Senate.

"We underestimated the degree of anger associated with that," Fischer said, adding the government should have cracked down much earlier on loopholes allowing abuses of parliamentary benefits such as travel allowances.
"Colston and Wik gave us an awful April."

Prime Minister John Howard had also supported Colston's appointment to the post of Senate deputy president and approved the granting of extra benefits and staff after Colston defected from Labor, changing the Senate balance of power.
"The recovery from that particular turning point and the anger people felt ... is taking time to rinse through the system," said Fischer.

Fischer said the government has also been slow to ease community concerns over the land rights row prompted by last December's High Court ruling in the "Wik case" that Aborigines retained rights to land leased to farmers.

Fischer, who heads the junior coalition partner, the National Party, will spend much of the winter break in the party's rural heartland seeking to regain lost support. Parliament broke up last week and resumes on August 25.
"This government will spend much of July getting back to the grassroots," Fischer said.

"We will be taking the opportunity of this winter recess to go back to the people, feet on the ground, and that's always the best thing you can do in a recess, is to get out there and listen and be guided by what the feedback is.
"We have delivered a great deal -- lower interest rates, a budget moving to surplus," he said.
The next election is due by May, 1999, but is increasingly expected by late 1998.
A poll in the national daily, the Australian, on Tuesday showed the coalition's support well down from its election high.
The poll put the government's popularity at 42 percent, against Labor's 37 percent.
This compares with the coalition's winning vote of 47.3 percent in the last election and Labor's 38.8 percent.
